title: Siddur close: prayer shapes the day
hookLine: morning, afternoon, evening, Shabbat, festivals: the prayer book is a map of time
tomorrow: Elul: the king in the field

lines: FROM THE ROOSTER TO THE ROAD.
cards: Back on day five hundred thirty-eight, you opened a book. A siddur. The word means order.
For a hundred and four days you've walked it, roughly in the order it's prayed. The morning blessings and the rooster. The warm-up psalms.
The Shema with a hand over the eyes. The Amidah on your feet. Kaddish, Aleinu, the afternoon pause, the evening's shelter.
Shabbat welcomed like a bride. The festivals, the Days of Awe, and this last week, the prayers that live outside the book.

teach.b: Step back and look at the whole siddur, and it isn't really organized by topic. It's organized by time, a map of the clock and the calendar.
Morning, afternoon, evening: three services a day.
The Talmud links them to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Genesis gives Isaac a beautiful moment for the afternoon: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide."
A psalm names all three times in a row: "Evening, and morning, and at noonday, will I complain, and moan; and He hath heard my voice."

teach.h: THE WEEK, THE MONTH, THE YEAR.
teach.b: Then the week: six weekdays with their requests, and Shabbat, when the requests go quiet and the Amidah becomes one long breath of holiness. Then the month, with the new moon.
Then the year: the festivals with Hallel, the Days of Awe with their own thick book. Then a life: a prayer for a journey, a blessing after food, the Kaddish after a death.
Open the siddur anywhere and the first question it answers is: what time is it? That's the deep idea.

Prayer in this tradition isn't mainly something you do when you feel like it. It's a rhythm laid over time, so the day itself has a shape. The day wakes into thanks, pauses in the middle, and lies down into shelter.
The prayers come back around until the day is held by them, the way a riverbank holds the river. Next comes the year itself, beginning with Elul.

how: Observant Jews pray three services daily, Shacharit, Mincha and Maariv, with added prayers for Shabbat, the new moon and festivals, all laid out in the siddur; many others keep one or two prayers, like Modeh Ani or the Shema at bedtime.

games.q: you open a siddur at random. what's the first question it answers about the page you're on?
o: what time is it: which hour, day or season?
games.why: the siddur is a map of time: every section belongs to an hour, a day or a season.

practice: Look back over the whole walk, the morning blessings, the rooster's understanding, the Shema, the Amidah's open my lips, Birkat HaMazon, the evening's spread over us, the traveler's prayer, five words for someone sick, and pick the one that stayed with you.
Decide when in your day it would live: morning, midday, a meal, or night. If you pray, say it now, once, slowly; if not, hold it as a line to live by.

wordCard.voice: Siddur. Order: the prayer book's name, read today as a map of time, day, week, month, year and a life.
